title: How Shortlist works
description: Questions about this app itself: how it scores postings, keeps data safe and stays honest. The answers point at the code in this repo.

cards.prompt: Why does Shortlist compute fit scores in code instead of asking a language model for a number?
cards.answer:
A score that comes from code is **repeatable and explainable**. The same posting and profile always give the same total, every point belongs to a named part with a reason, and the parts add up to the total.

The tool Shortlist replaced asked a model to write scores, and most of its breakdowns broke their own caps or did not add up. In code, the rubric has tests at every band boundary, and a `rubricVersion` on each result says which rules produced it.

A model can still help at the edges, for example drafting text a person edits.
keyPoints: Every point has a part and a reason
Parts always sum to the total
Rubric is tested at its boundaries

cards.prompt: Explain the recency gate. Why does a posting with a high score still get held?
cards.answer:
Fresh postings get the most replies, so the bar to apply rises with age:

| Age | Minimum score |
| --- | --- |
| under 12 hours | 65 |
| 12 to 24 hours | 70 |
| 24 to 48 hours | 75 |
| 48 to 72 hours | 85 |

A score below a band's bar is held, not skipped: only its age keeps it back. From 72 hours to 30 days every posting is held, with a reminder to check it is still open, because new-grad postings often stay open for weeks. Past 30 days it is skipped, unless a person checked it is still open; age alone never skips a checked posting. The 30-day limit is a profile setting. A score below 65 is skipped at any age, and a posting with **no known date** is held rather than guessed, because a wrong date is worse than no date.
keyPoints: From 72 hours to 30 days it is held; past 30 days skipped unless checked
Unknown age is held, not guessed
Holding is reversible; a person can still apply

cards.prompt: Two postings at the same company are "Software Engineer" and "Software Engineer Intern". Why must the duplicate check keep them apart?
cards.answer:
The old scanner normalized titles by stripping words like "junior" and "intern", so the internship and the full-time role produced the same key and one was dropped as a duplicate.

Shortlist keeps the **level** in the key: company, normalized title and level (intern, new grad, junior, mid, senior). It also matches words on boundaries, so "Internal Tools Engineer" is not read as an internship.
keyPoints: Normalizing titles can merge different roles
The level stays part of the key

cards.answer:
Shortlist never submits anything. It can get an application ready (answers chosen, cover letter drafted) but only a person can send it. If "ready" and "sent" were one status, follow-up reminders would start counting from a day nothing was sent.

Recording `applied` only when you confirm you submitted keeps the follow-up dates and response rates true.
keyPoints: The tool prepares, the person submits
Follow-ups count from the real submit date

cards.prompt: Jobs live in a JSONL file that both the app and command-line scripts write. How does a save avoid losing data?
cards.answer:
Three rules:

1. **Readers take the last line for an id.** A script may append a newer copy of a row instead of rewriting the file.
2. **Writers replace an id in place and keep every line they cannot parse**, so a save never deletes data it does not understand.
3. **Writes are atomic**: the new file is written beside the old one and renamed over it, so nobody reads half a file.

The dev server also runs writes to the same file one at a time, so two saves arriving together cannot drop a row.
keyPoints: Last copy of an id wins on read
Writes to one file are serialized

cards.prompt: The dev server exposes the private data folder at /__local. What stops another website open in the same browser from reading it?
cards.answer:
Several checks, because each covers a different attack:

- **Loopback only**: requests from another machine are refused even if the server listens on the network.
- **Host header**: must be localhost, which stops DNS rebinding (a hostile domain that resolves to 127.0.0.1).
- **Origin header**: a request from another origin is refused.
- **Custom header**: every request needs `x-shortlist-local: 1`. A cross-site page cannot add a custom header without a CORS preflight, and nothing approves it for a foreign origin.

The middleware is also only part of the dev server, never the production build.

cards.prompt: The public demo was written on one day, but its postings always look a few hours old. How?
cards.answer: The sample data records the moment it was written for. When the demo loads it, every timestamp is moved forward by the time since then, rounded to the minute, and plain dates by the number of calendar days. Relative ages stay exactly as written, so the recency gate and follow-up reminders behave the same on any day.
keyPoints: Shift by elapsed time on load

cards.prompt: Shortlist is local-first for one person. What would have to change for a team of career coaches to share it?
cards.answer:
The engine would stay the same; the data layer is what changes.

- Files on one machine become a database with one owner per row and access rules.
- The dev middleware becomes a real API with sign-in, since "localhost only" no longer identifies the user.
- Concurrent edits need versioning or last-write-wins rules per field.
- Private data now leaves the machine, so it needs encryption at rest, retention rules and a way to export or delete it.

Keeping the engine pure (no storage, no network) is what makes this a data-layer change rather than a rewrite.
keyPoints: Engine unchanged because it is pure
Privacy obligations once data leaves the machine
